\[
r_g(i) = \begin{cases}
  g + \operatorname{sign}(i - g)\, \sigma_r\, f_d\!\left(\frac{\lvert i - g \rvert}{\sigma_r}\right) & \lvert i - g \rvert \le \sigma_r \\
  g + \operatorname{sign}(i - g) \left(f_e(\lvert i - g \rvert - \sigma_r) + \sigma_r\right) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\qquad
f_d(x) = x^{\alpha},\ f_e(a) = \beta a
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(r_g\): The remapping function around g
- \(g\): The Gaussian pyramid coefficient, the local brightness
- \(\sigma_r\): The largest difference that counts as detail
- \(\alpha\): The detail power
- \(\beta\): The edge factor

Paris et al. compute each coefficient of the output's Laplacian pyramid on its own. g is the value of the Gaussian pyramid at that place and level. They remap the image around g with r_g and copy the coefficient from the Laplacian pyramid of the remapped image. Differences from g up to sigma_r are details, scaled by f_d. Larger ones are edges, scaled by f_e. Because the remapping is centered on the local brightness, an edge stays an edge and makes no halo. To stop noise from growing when alpha is below 1, f_d blends back to x for differences under 1 to 2 percent of the largest intensity. Aubry et al. compute the remapped pyramids only for a few values of g and interpolate between them.
